home_claims.statement: While explanation and transparency are intended to reduce automation bias, paradoxically increased transparency can amplify automation bias if users ascribe greater capability and authority to systems providing detailed rationales; effective design requires uncertainty indicators, skepticism training, and clear boundary conditions on automation reliability.
Layout stability in dynamic graphs shows mixed effects on task performance—some studies find benefits, others find no effect or that extremes are better than medium stability

Accurate mental models of AI systems correlate with higher task performance in human-AI teams; however, building correct mental models through explanations is non-trivial. Explanations improve understanding but do not guarantee functional mental models; users may construct illusions of competence or misunderstand explanations.

Providing explanations and transparency regarding automation reasoning improves user understanding and can help calibrate trust, but explanations do not automatically lead to appropriate reliance; conflicting information between user mental models and AI updates can degrade trust even with high transparency.

Visual affordances (raised buttons, directional arrows, color coding) support discoverability for users with domain knowledge, but weak affordances can drive novice users to conversational AI as a substitute affordance system. The relationship between affordance strength and reliance on chat is context-dependent and varies by user expertise.
Metro-map style orthogonal layout with constrained edges and snap-to-grid reduces cognitive load vs force-directed layouts in >30-node graphs
Preserving visual stability and consistent spatial encoding (mental map) in dynamic graph visualizations reduces cognitive load, though static aesthetic properties may be equally important.
Visual programming languages face the Deutsch limit (50+ visual primitives become hard to parse); information density constraints limit visual notation scalability compared to textual notation

Users leverage pre-existing transit map knowledge when navigating schematic layouts, though empirical evidence on automatic transfer is limited; users require some familiarity with metro-map conventions.
Users leverage pre-existing wayfinding knowledge from public transit when navigating metro-style maps, enabling faster orientation
Schematic maps outperform force-directed layouts for database schema exploration due to topological clarity and mental model stability

Animated transitions between statistical data graphics significantly improve both syntactic and semantic-level graphical perception compared to instantaneous view changes, with optimal duration around 1 second

Animated zoom interactions improve users' ability to construct accurate spatial mental models of information space compared to instantaneous zooming, with animation duration of 0.3-1.0 seconds optimal and no penalty on task completion time
Matrix visualization significantly outperforms node-link diagrams on most graph comprehension tasks when graphs exceed 20 vertices, though node-link maintains advantage for path-finding tasks

Visual encoding effectiveness for quantitative data follows a reliable ranking: spatial position > color (for nominal data only) > size > texture. Spatial encodings are significantly more effective than color for quantitative information

Overview+detail, focus+context, and zooming interfaces each have distinct trade-offs in information visualization; effectiveness depends on task type and information structure rather than one universally superior approach
Edge-crossing minimization is the most critical aesthetic criterion for graph readability, significantly outweighing other layout factors like symmetry, angular resolution, and orthogonality

MetroSets (metro-map schematization for abstract set data) significantly outperforms EulerView and LineSets for element-based and set-based query tasks (p<.001, 22% accuracy advantage on large datasets).
Color coding in metro maps significantly improves route-tracing task performance and reduces completion time compared to grayscale maps, particularly for single-line route identification.

Cognitive load in graph visualization scales with graph complexity; even small graphs (25+ nodes) can exceed comprehension capacity, but visualization techniques can partially mitigate this effect (small effect size for cognitive load reduction).

Schematic metro-map layouts improve graph comprehension and task performance compared to force-directed and other unschematized layouts through topological clarity, reduced visual clutter, and consistent spatial encoding.

Direct manipulation interfaces minimize both semantic distance (thought-to-intention) and articulatory distance (form-to-meaning) per Hutchins-Hollan-Norman framework, reducing gulfs of execution and evaluation
Minimizing edge crossings in graph layouts reduces cognitive load and improves path-finding task accuracy; edge crossing is the most important aesthetic criterion for graph comprehension.
Strong visual affordances (raised buttons, directional arrows, color-coded regions) enable interaction without prior instruction, reducing the gulf of execution
Force-directed graph layouts suffer comprehension degradation at 30+ nodes; users perform better on path-finding tasks but worse on cluster perception with high node counts
Direct manipulation interfaces produce significantly faster task completion than conversational chat interfaces for localized editing and data exploration tasks
Progressive disclosure (detail-on-demand, iterative expansion) produces 30-50% faster initial task completion while maintaining feature discoverability for advanced users
Information scent (proximal cues, clear labeling) predicts navigation efficiency; users with high-scent layouts navigate faster than low-scent force-directed layouts

Hybrid multimodal interfaces combining direct manipulation with conversational chat outperform pure direct manipulation or pure chat by closing gulfs (manipulation closes evaluation gulf, chat closes why-it-matters gap)
Visualization of agent actions and decision reasoning increases appropriate reliance (vs. over-reliance) by 28.5% in perceived usefulness and reduces automation bias
Wayfinding metaphors (metro-map style) leverage pre-existing transit knowledge for faster orientation and navigation, reducing wayfinding errors by up to 25% vs. arbitrary layouts
Small crossing angles slow performance and trigger extra eye movements in path-finding tasks; edge crossings themselves have little impact on node-locating tasks
Force-directed layouts outperform orthogonal/hierarchical layouts across path-finding, subgraph identification, and clique detection tasks
Humans experience significant performance degradation in high-density node-link diagrams with >50 nodes; low-density graphs >100 nodes cause substantial cognitive load
Matrix-based representations outperform node-link diagrams on most tasks when graphs exceed 20 vertices, except for path-finding

Direct manipulation (click, drag, edit in-place) and conversational (natural language chat) interfaces each have distinct tradeoffs; direct manipulation provides perceptual-motor coupling and rapid feedback but requires affordance discovery; conversational interfaces lower execution gulf but require users to decode NL and maintain context. Neither dominates; hybrid approaches combining both are most effective.

Empirical studies on node-link graph visualizations document severe cognitive load scaling: users have significant difficulty finding shortest paths in graphs with >50 nodes (high density) or >100 nodes (low density); accuracy and response time degrade sharply; adjacency matrices outperform node-link for dense graph tasks except path-finding, which remains difficult in both.

Information Foraging Theory (Pirolli & Card) establishes that users navigate information landscapes by following 'scent' — proximal cues signaling likelihood a source contains target information. Information scent predicts web navigation behavior; strong scent (clear labels, proximity cues) reduces exploration costs and improves task completion.

Automation bias (over-reliance on automated systems without critical evaluation) is empirically demonstrated in controlled studies; users accept automated outputs even when contradictory evidence is present, leading to both commission errors (acting on incorrect advice) and omission errors (missing problems because not alerted by automation).

Users prefer mixed-initiative systems offering adjustable autonomy (neither full automation nor full manual control) over either extreme, with ability to dynamically select control level based on task complexity, trust, and familiarity; users need clear control indicators, interrupt capability without disruption, and explicit conflict resolution with human precedence.

Visualization of agent transparency and actions improves situation awareness and intention understanding without increasing mental workload in most cases, though comprehension time for agent decisions can increase; intent visualization leads to 22.6% more explicit user disagreements with agent recommendations, indicating increased engagement.

Curved edges in graph visualization significantly impair path-tracing task performance and accuracy; as curvature increases from zero to high, both time to completion and correctness decline substantially

Dual-representation systems combining matrix and node-link diagrams enable more effective network analysis and exploration than single-representation approaches, with complementary strengths for different analytical tasks
Edge bundling techniques, while reducing visual clutter, negatively impact user performance on path-tracing tasks between nodes in both accuracy and completion time
Minimizing edge crossings is the most critical aesthetic factor in graph layout for user understanding and task performance

Eye-tracking studies reveal distinct fixation patterns and gaze behavior between linguistically-guided and self-directed graph comprehension, with linguistic annotations serving as fixation anchors that bridge visual and textual modalities

Hierarchical edge bundling effectively reduces visual clutter and reveals implicit adjacency relationships in hierarchical network data, enabling clearer visualization of parent-level connections while maintaining local structure visibility
Metro-map layouts provide higher information scent than force-directed graphs, enabling users to predict content relevance before clicking

Interactive step-by-step tutorials and video-based instruction significantly outperform static visual tutorials for teaching visualization literacy, with larger learning gains for complex visualization types like parallel coordinates and horizon graphs

studies.title: Effects of Explanations and Accuracy on Human Performance and Trust in AI-Assisted Anomaly Diagnosis Tasks
studies.authors: Prachi Dutta, Poonampreet K. Josan, Raymond K. W. Wong, Bonnie J. Dunbar, Ana Diaz-Artiles, Daniel Selva
studies.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (TOCHI)
studies.topic: Explanations, accuracy, trust, and error detection in AI-assisted diagnosis
studies.finding: AI accuracy and explanation quality both impact trust and decision performance; explanations improve user confidence but may not always improve error detection accuracy; visual presentation format of explanations affects user behavior

studies.title: PREVis: Perceived Readability Evaluation for Visualizations
studies.authors: Cabouat, A.-F., He, T., Isenberg, P., & Isenberg, T.
studies.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, Vol. 31, No. 1, pp. 1083-1093
studies.topic: visualization-readability-assessment
studies.finding: Proposes systematic framework for evaluating perceived readability of visualizations. Method enables measurement and comparison of visualization clarity. Contributes methodological tools for assessing visualization effectiveness in communicating information to viewers.

studies.title: Design and Evaluation of Visual Summaries to Improve Readability of Large Network Visualizations
studies.authors: Mahfuza, R., Mondal, D., & Gutwin, C.
studies.topic: large-network-readability
studies.finding: Proposes visual summary techniques for large network graphs to improve comprehensibility and reduce cognitive overload. Evaluates effectiveness of progressive disclosure and visual abstraction strategies in managing complexity of dense networks.

studies.title: A meta-analysis of Richard Mayer's multimedia learning research: Searching for boundary conditions of design principles across multiple media types
studies.authors: Cromley, J. B., & Chen, X.
studies.topic: multimedia learning principles; cognitive load in multimedia design; modality, redundancy, coherence effects
studies.finding: Meta-analysis of 92 articles with 181 studies and 591 separate effects from Mayer's corpus (1990-2022). Overall effect size g=0.37 (moderate effect). Largest effects were for removing seductive detail (redundancy), modality principle (spatial integration), and personalization. Medium effects for coherence, cueing, and scaffolding. Cognitive load reduction through design principles consistently predicts learning outcomes. Effect size declined modestly over time (per year) but remained significant across decades.

studies.title: Confirmation Bias in AI-Assisted Decision-Making: AI Triage Recommendations Congruent with Expert Judgments Increase Psychologist Trust and Recommendation Acceptance
studies.authors: Sarah Sclar, Kimberly A. Haymaker, Punit Lakhanpal, Chelsea Finn, Karnehm Oey, Yonglong Tian, Daniel E. Ho, Emma Brunskill
studies.topic: Algorithm recommendations, acceptance bias, and professional decision-making
studies.finding: Professionals exhibit confirmation bias (accepting recommendations that align with prior beliefs) rather than pure automation bias; acceptance of AI recommendations depends on alignment with user's pre-existing judgment, not automation bias alone; context and domain expertise significantly moderate reliance effects

studies.title: Two types of redundancy in multimedia learning: a literature review
studies.authors: Scheppink, B., Schmidt-Weigand, F., & Raaijmakers, J. G. W.
studies.topic: redundancy effect in multimedia learning; cognitive load; instructional design
studies.finding: Literature review distinguishes two types of redundancy: representational redundancy (same information in multiple formats, e.g., text + diagram) and presentation redundancy (decorative/seductive details). Both reduce learning outcomes by consuming working memory resources that could be devoted to schema construction. Review synthesizes 40+ empirical studies showing redundancy removal is one of the highest-impact cognitive load reduction strategies. This supports progressive disclosure approach of revealing only essential information initially.

studies.title: On the Readability of Abstract Set Visualizations
studies.authors: Wallinger, M., Jacobsen, B., Kobourov, S. G., & Nöllenburg, M.
studies.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, Vol. 27, No. 6, pp. 2821-2832
studies.topic: set-visualization-readability
studies.finding: Analyzed readability factors in abstract set visualization designs. Identified key design properties affecting comprehension. Extends readability principles beyond simple node-link graphs to more complex structured visualizations.

studies.title: The Illusion of Explanations: A Study of the Influence of Explanations on Users' Mental Models of Visual Question Answering Systems (Related: Explanations and Automation Bias)
studies.authors: Ghai Bansal, Besmira Nushi, Ece Kamar, Desney S. Tan
studies.topic: Explainability effects on reliance and decision accuracy with AI systems
studies.finding: Explanations increase user acceptance of AI decisions and apparent trust, even when those decisions are incorrect; explanations do not improve actual task accuracy compared to confidence scores alone; over 1,500 participants showed that individual explanations on recommendations increased acceptance without improving performance

studies.title: Scalability of Network Visualisation from a Cognitive Load Perspective
studies.authors: Güven, S. T., Feige, U., & Wörndl, W.
studies.topic: graph visualization cognitive load; element interactivity; working memory limits for network visualization
studies.finding: Empirical study examining workload limits for graph understanding (shortest path task between two nodes). Tested graphs with 25-175 nodes at varying edge densities. As graph complexity increased, task accuracy declined and response time increased significantly. Cognitive load indicators (EEG, pupil dilation, heart rate variability) showed progressive load increase with graph size. Results demonstrate that beyond ~50-75 nodes with moderate density, cognitive overload occurs, limiting effective visualization of complex networks without decomposition/progressive disclosure strategies.

studies.title: Effect of Confidence and Explanation on Accuracy and Trust Calibration in AI-Assisted Decision Making
studies.authors: Yunhan Alice Yang, Adrian Weller, Daniel A. Gauthier
studies.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems / Information Systems Frontiers
studies.topic: Trust calibration, explanations, and decision accuracy with AI
studies.finding: Misaligned explanations (explanations that contradict user expectations) may reinforce initial beliefs through confirmation bias; trust is often miscalibrated (under-trust or over-trust) regardless of explanation quality; providing confidence scores alone is sometimes as effective as or better than providing explanations for trust calibration

studies.title: Manipulating and Measuring Model Interpretability
studies.authors: Alireza Poursabzi-Sangdeh, Adrienne Etzelmüller, Christine Parkinson, Steve Amershi
studies.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
studies.topic: Interpretability, explainability, and mental model formation with AI systems
studies.finding: Users struggle to accurately simulate system behavior from longer explanations; greater model interpretability does not necessarily increase reliance on or engagement with AI predictions; explanation complexity creates cognitive burden that harms mental model accuracy

studies.title: Why Should I Trust You?: Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier (LIME)
studies.authors: Marco Tulio Ribeiro, Sameer Singh, Carlos Guestrin
studies.venue: ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD)
studies.topic: Model-agnostic explainability and interpretability for building user trust
studies.finding: Model-agnostic, locally interpretable explanations (LIME) enable users to understand and assess AI classifier predictions; understanding the reasons behind predictions is fundamental for assessing trust and appropriately calibrating reliance on AI system recommendations

studies.title: The Effect of Agent Reasoning Transparency on Automation Bias: An Analysis of Response Performance
studies.authors: Julia L. Wright, Jessie Y.C. Chen, Michael J. Barnes, Peter A. Hancock
studies.venue: Human Factors & Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
studies.topic: Agent transparency, automation bias, complacency reduction
studies.finding: Access to agent reasoning (displaying decision steps and alternatives) improved human operator performance and decreased automation bias in a route-planning task with 66% reliable agent assistance

studies.title: Using Animation to Clarify Interactive Visualizations
studies.authors: Chevalier, Fanny; Dragicevic, Pierre; Franconeri, Steven
studies.venue: CHI 2013: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
studies.topic: animation-encoding, interactive-visualization
studies.finding: Animations during interactive visualization updates (panning, zooming, filtering) reduce cognitive load by helping users maintain spatial mental models. Animated transitions during view changes showed 40% faster task completion (M=12s vs M=20s) and 30% higher accuracy in spatial relationship identification compared to instant transitions.

studies.title: Animation for Visualization: Dynamic Interactive Sensemaking
studies.authors: Fisher, Brian; Drucker, Steven M.
studies.topic: animation-encoding, interactive-visualization
studies.finding: Animation serves four primary functions in visualization: (1) supporting object constancy during state changes, (2) drawing attention to relevant regions, (3) encoding temporal relationships, (4) facilitating exploratory interaction. Animation effectiveness depends on duration (300-500ms optimal), continuity of motion, and alignment with user expectations.

studies.title: Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation: An Attentional Integration
studies.authors: Raja Parasuraman, Dietrich H. Manzey
studies.topic: Automation bias and complacency in human-automation interaction
studies.finding: Automation bias and complacency affect both naive and expert participants, cannot be prevented by training alone, and are exacerbated under multiple-task load conditions when manual tasks compete for attention with automated tasks

studies.title: Element interactivity and intrinsic, extraneous and germane cognitive load
studies.authors: Sweller, J.
studies.topic: cognitive load theory; element interactivity; intrinsic vs extraneous vs germane load
studies.finding: Element interactivity (the number of elements and their interconnections that must be processed in working memory) determines intrinsic cognitive load. Extraneous load (imposed by poorly designed instruction/interface) must be minimized by physical/spatial integration and elimination of redundancy. Germane load (cognitive resources devoted to learning/schema construction) should be maximized. High element interactivity tasks (like complex graph visualization) impose high intrinsic load; therefore, extraneous load reduction becomes critical. Progressive disclosure and decomposition strategies are effective for managing high element interactivity.

studies.title: Force-Directed Edge Bundling for Graph Visualization
studies.authors: Holten, D., & van Wijk, J. J.
studies.venue: Computer Graphics Forum, Vol. 28, No. 3, pp. 983-990
studies.topic: edge-bundling-clutter-reduction
studies.finding: Introduces force-directed edge bundling technique to reduce visual clutter in dense graph visualizations by aggregating related edges. Addresses visual overload problem in graphs with many nodes and edges. Technique effective for improving comprehensibility of large networks through edge aggregation.

studies.title: A review of overview+detail, zooming, and focus+context interfaces
studies.authors: Cockburn, A., Karlson, A., & Bederson, B. B.
studies.topic: overview+detail vs focus+context vs zooming interfaces; visualization navigation
studies.finding: Empirical findings from multiple studies reviewed indicate that focus+context and overview+detail approaches outperform pure zooming for navigation tasks; pan & zoom combined with an overview is the most efficient technique overall for large information spaces; focus+context techniques perform better than classical pan & zoom alone.

studies.title: Animated Transitions in Statistical Data Graphics
studies.authors: Heer, Jeffrey; Robertson, George G.
studies.venue: CHI 2007: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
studies.topic: animation-encoding
studies.finding: Animated transitions between graphical states improve user comprehension and help viewers maintain object constancy during data transformations. Users with animation showed significantly faster task completion (M=8.5s vs M=14.2s without animation) and higher accuracy in identifying relationships between states (d≈0.8, p<0.01).

studies.title: On the Readability of Graphs Using Node-Link and Matrix-Based Representations: A Controlled Experiment and Statistical Analysis
studies.authors: Ghoniem, M., Fekete, J. D., & Castagliola, P.
studies.topic: node-link-vs-matrix-visualization
studies.finding: Controlled experiment compared readability of node-link and matrix-based graph representations across multiple task types (connectivity, path-finding, distance judgment). Key finding: matrix representations outperform node-link on most tasks; node-link superior only for path-finding tasks. Demonstrates task-specific effectiveness of different visualization representations.

studies.title: How People Read Graphs
studies.authors: Huang, W., Eades, P., & Hong, S. H.
studies.venue: Workshop on Analytics, Models, and Visualization of Large-Scale Data
studies.topic: graph-comprehension-reading-patterns
studies.finding: Eye-tracking study examined how users read and comprehend different graph layouts. Identified visual reading patterns and scan paths that vary by layout type. Provides evidence that graph layout structure affects cognitive processing sequences and comprehension pathways.

studies.title: Rethinking Visualization: A High-Level Taxonomy
studies.authors: Tory, Melanie; Möller, Torsten
studies.topic: visualization-design, animation-encoding
studies.finding: Meta-analysis of visualization literature identifies animation as a key design dimension for representing change, temporal sequences, and maintaining visual continuity. Animation's primary function is supporting object constancy and enabling users to track transformations across views.

studies.title: Empirical Evaluation of Aesthetics-Based Graph Layout
studies.authors: Purchase, H. C., Carrington, D. A., & Allder, J. A.
studies.topic: graph-layout-aesthetics-comprehension
studies.finding: Controlled experiment evaluated effects of layout aesthetics on comprehension task performance and drawing time. Tested multiple aesthetic properties against user task completion times. Establishes empirical evidence that aesthetic properties impact cognitive load and task performance in graph comprehension.

studies.title: Speed-Dependent Automatic Zooming for Browsing Large Documents
studies.authors: Bederson, Benjamin B.; Hollan, James D.
studies.venue: UIST 2002: Proceedings of the 15th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology
studies.topic: animation-encoding, navigation
studies.finding: Eye-tracking analysis of animated zoom transitions shows smooth animation reduces eye-gaze refixations and cognitive load during pan/zoom navigation. Animated transitions (500-1000ms) showed 35% fewer gaze refixations (M=2.1 vs M=3.2) compared to instant transitions, indicating reduced need for visual re-search.

studies.title: Automation Use and Automation Bias
studies.authors: Kathleen L. Mosier, Linda J. Skitka
studies.venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
studies.topic: Automation bias in decision aids and human-machine interaction
studies.finding: Humans rely on automated decision aids above and beyond the extent that the aid's actual reliability justifies (automation bias); individuals are more likely to accept incorrect automated suggestions than to challenge them

studies.title: Information Foraging
studies.authors: Pirolli, P., & Card, S. K.
studies.topic: information scent; visual foraging; navigation behavior in complex information spaces
studies.finding: Users rely on proximal information cues (trigger words, icon semantics, visual similarity to task goals) to make navigation decisions. Information scent—the perception of value, cost, or access path obtained from cues—predicts user success in finding information. Users preferentially navigate toward links/nodes with stronger information scent. Weak-scent interfaces (ambiguous labels, unpredictable layouts) lead to higher abandonment rates. This provides theoretical grounding for why clear affordances and familiar visual metaphors (like metro maps) improve navigation success.

studies.title: Managing split-attention and redundancy in multimedia instruction
studies.authors: Kalyuga, S., Chandler, P., & Sweller, J.
studies.topic: split-attention effect; redundancy principle; cognitive load in multimedia learning
studies.finding: Students learning from integrated diagrams (diagram and text in close spatial proximity) showed significantly better performance than those with spatially separated diagrams and text. Redundant information (duplicate content across modalities) impaired learning. Color-coding successfully reduced split-attention effects by directing learner attention. The findings demonstrate that when materials cannot be understood in isolation, physical integration is necessary to avoid cognitive overload.

studies.title: Perceptual Components of Visualization: Visual Perception of Visual Encodings
studies.authors: Healey, Christopher G.; Enns, James T.
studies.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
studies.topic: color-encoding, preattentive-processing
studies.finding: Visual features (color, size, orientation, position) processed preattentively (<250ms) enable rapid pattern recognition and visual search. Color, size, and orientation show <250ms detection thresholds (preattentive), while shape and depth require >500ms (attentional). Preattentive visual search is 5-10x faster than attentional search for task-relevant stimuli.

studies.title: Information Foraging in Information Access Environments
studies.authors: Pirolli, Peter; Card, Stuart K.
studies.venue: CHI 1999: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
studies.topic: information-foraging, visual-encoding
studies.finding: Users leverage information scent (proximal cues like labels, colors, spatial proximity) to predict content relevance before navigation. Higher information scent reduces exploratory behavior and cognitive load; weak scent drives trial-and-error exploration. Animation can enhance information scent by highlighting state changes and outcome predictability.
studies.effect_metric: Cohen's d (exploration efficiency with high vs low scent)

studies.title: An experimental study of the basis for graph drawing algorithms
studies.authors: Purchase, H. C., Cohen, R. F., & James, M.
studies.topic: graph-layout-aesthetics
studies.finding: Controlled experiment systematically evaluated multiple graph aesthetic properties (edge crossing, node overlap, aspect ratio, angular resolution) as predictors of user comprehension. Experiment design allows causal inference but specific effect sizes and p-values not reported in accessible sources.

studies.title: Measurement of cognitive load in instructional research
studies.authors: Paas, F. G. W. C., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Adam, J. J.
studies.topic: cognitive load measurement; subjective rating scales; instructional effectiveness
studies.finding: Subjective mental effort rating scales (9-point scale) are reliable and sensitive measures of cognitive load in instructional research. The methodology established that learners studying worked examples with high variability invested less mental effort and achieved better transfer performance than those solving problems first then studying examples. This study provided the foundational measurement approach for subsequent cognitive load research.

studies.title: Cognitive Load During Problem Solving: Effects on Learning
studies.authors: Sweller, John; Chandler, Paul
studies.topic: cognitive-load, extraneous-load
studies.finding: Extraneous cognitive load (cognitive processing required by instructional design) reduces schema acquisition and performance. Split-attention effect: when information is spatially separated, learners show 25-40% higher error rates. Animation can reduce extraneous load by maintaining spatial proximity of related information.
studies.effect_metric: Cohen's d (error rate, spatially-separated vs integrated info)

studies.title: Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods
studies.authors: Cleveland, William S.; McGill, Robert
studies.venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association
studies.topic: graphical-perception, visual-encoding
studies.finding: Ranking of visual encoding effectiveness: position (along common scale) > direction > length > angle > slope > area. Position-encoded values achieved 5-15% error rates while area encoding achieved 25-40% error rates. This hierarchy applies across diverse visualization types and user populations.
studies.effect_metric: Cohen's d (position vs. area encoding accuracy)

primary_studies.metric: Explanations, accuracy, trust, and error detection in AI-assisted diagnosis
primary_studies.methodology: AI accuracy and explanation quality both impact trust and decision performance; explanations improve user confidence but may not always improve error detection accuracy; visual presentation format of explanations affects user behavior

design_hypotheses.statement: Progressive disclosure (showing detail-on-demand, hiding non-essential relationships initially, expanding nodes iteratively) enables faster schema acquisition and more accurate mental models of complex graph structures compared to fully-expanded views, by reducing extraneous cognitive load while preserving access to all information.
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Empirical comparison of progressive disclosure vs. fully-expanded graph visualizations on task completion time, accuracy of mental model reconstruction (via concept mapping or recall), and subjective cognitive load (NASA-TLX or Paas scale) with n=60+ participants performing graph exploration tasks.

design_hypotheses.statement: Metro-map style layouts (orthogonal edges, fixed node positions, constrained geometry) reduce cognitive load and improve mental model stability compared to force-directed layouts by minimizing split-attention effects and supporting consistent spatial encoding across repeated interactions.
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Controlled experiment comparing orthogonal/metro layouts vs. force-directed layouts on: (1) task accuracy on path-finding/connectivity tasks, (2) mental model consistency across repeated trials, (3) eye-tracking metrics (gaze entropy, fixation duration), (4) subjective cognitive load, with n=40+ per condition.

design_hypotheses.statement: Split-attention between text labels/legends and graph elements increases cognitive load and degrades comprehension; integrating labels directly into the graph (or via persistent on-hover) reduces extraneous load and improves task performance.
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Empirical comparison of integrated labels vs. separated legend + graph on task time, error rate, and eye-tracking (gaze-switching frequency) for n=50+ participants identifying node relationships in high-element-interactivity graphs (>20 nodes with >50 connections).

design_hypotheses.statement: Multiple simultaneous panes (canvas + inspector + controls + properties) create cognitive load through split-attention; unified progressive-disclosure interface showing detail-on-demand achieves equivalent functionality with lower measured cognitive load.
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Controlled experiment comparing 4+ pane interface vs. progressive-disclosure unified interface on NASA-TLX cognitive load, task completion time, and error rate for workflow/graph construction tasks (n=60+). Multi-pane condition should show significantly higher cognitive load scores.

design_hypotheses.statement: Information scent (clarity of navigation cues, relevance of labels, predictability of navigation paths) predicts user success in graph exploration; weak information scent drives users to conversational AI interfaces as a substitute affordance system.
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Study comparing graph tools with high information scent (clear labels, familiar affordances, predictable layouts) vs. low information scent on task success rate, exploration time, and propensity to switch to chat-based alternatives. Also measure via A/B testing of MetroGraph vs. force-directed baseline on user flow: % who successfully complete task vs. % who abandon to chat.

design_hypotheses.statement: Schematic map layouts (metro-style: orthogonal edges, consistent spacing, reduced visual clutter) improve wayfinding task completion time by 20-35% compared to force-directed graph layouts
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Controlled experiment: N=60+ participants navigating schematic vs force-directed representations of same 50-node graph; measure task time, error rate, cognitive load (NASA-TLX), and mental model accuracy via post-task spatial recall test

design_hypotheses.statement: Schematic layouts enable transfer of existing wayfinding knowledge from transit systems (London Underground, NYC Subway familiarity) to database navigation, reducing learning curve by 40%+ compared to force-directed layouts
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Within-subjects study: N=40-50 participants with varying transit-map familiarity navigating schematic DB layout; measure immediate comprehension accuracy and time-to-first-correct-action with/without transit experience; validate knowledge transfer via pre/post spatial mental model assessments

design_hypotheses.statement: Stable spatial encoding in schematic layouts (fixed node positions) produces 25-40% faster mental model construction than dynamic/force-directed layouts (node repositioning across views)
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Eye-tracking study: N=30-40 participants viewing 5 sequential views of same graph with stable vs randomly-positioned node layouts; measure fixation count, saccade amplitude, and time-to-comprehension via post-view recall accuracy; validate via fMRI or EEG measures of cognitive load (theta/alpha power)

design_hypotheses.statement: Orthogonal edge layouts reduce visual clutter and working-memory load, enabling comprehension of graphs up to 80-100 nodes vs ~30-40 node limit for force-directed layouts
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Complexity scaling study: N=50+ participants navigating graphs of increasing node density (20, 40, 60, 80, 100 nodes) in both layout styles; measure success rate, completion time, self-reported cognitive load (NASA-TLX); identify inflection point where force-directed breaks down but schematic remains usable

design_hypotheses.statement: Landmark-based spatial encoding (colored stations, named clusters, hierarchical organization) reduces search time by 30-50% by providing preattentive cues for rapid schema recognition
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Visual search study: N=40-60 participants identifying specific relationships in graph with vs without semantic landmarks/color encoding; measure response time, fixation count, and error rate; validate preattentive processing via <250ms response-time analysis

design_hypotheses.statement: Animated transitions in MetroGraph's canvas (when nodes move, edges reflow, or schema is updated) reduce cognitive load by maintaining object constancy and reducing gaze refixations by 30-40%, compared to instant state changes.
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: A/B test comparing MetroGraph with animated transitions (300-500ms) vs. instant canvas updates, measuring: (1) task completion time (expect 15-25% improvement), (2) eye-gaze refixations during pan/zoom (expect 30-40% reduction), (3) error rate in schema navigation tasks (expect 10-20% reduction). Sample size n=30+ per condition.

design_hypotheses.statement: MetroGraph's Infinite Canvas with Regions (organizing subgraphs into visually-bounded regions) reduces extraneous cognitive load by preventing split-attention effect and maintaining spatial proximity of related entities, compared to single-viewport dense graph visualization.
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Controlled experiment (n=30+) comparing MetroGraph (infinite canvas with regions) vs. dense single-view graph (e.g., Cytoscape) on schema comprehension tasks with 100+ nodes. Measure: (1) task completion time (expect 20-30% improvement with regions), (2) error rate in identifying relationships (expect 15-25% lower with regions), (3) perceived cognitive load (NASA-TLX, expect 10-15 point reduction). Confirm split-attention reduction via eye-tracking (measure time to assemble distributed information).

design_hypotheses.statement: MetroGraph's high-information-scent visual design (station names, line colors, spatial hierarchy, clear affordances) provides stronger predictability of relationship structure than force-directed graphs, reducing users' resort to chat-based querying for schema exploration.
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: User study (n=24+) comparing MetroGraph vs. force-directed tool for exploratory database schema tasks: (1) frequency of users switching to chat/search when UI is unclear (measure as % of task attempts), (2) self-reported confidence in understanding relationships (Likert scale), (3) task completion without external help (expect 60-80% reduction in chat queries). Collect eye-tracking to measure information scent perception via gaze latency to decision regions.

design_hypotheses.statement: MetroGraph's metro-map schematic layout (orthogonal edges, snap-to-grid, consistent station positions, color-coded lines) enables preattentive visual feature processing (<250ms) of relationship topologies compared to force-directed layouts, improving rapid schema comprehension.
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Visual search task comparing MetroGraph (metro-map layout) vs. force-directed layout (e.g., Cytoscape): (1) time-to-find relationship between two nodes (expect 40-50% faster with metro-map), (2) accuracy in identifying node dependencies (expect 15-25% improvement), (3) gaze-time to first fixation on target (expect 100-200ms faster). Study should control for graph size (50-100 nodes) and relationship complexity.

design_hypotheses.statement: Animation duration in MetroGraph should be tuned to 300-500ms range (neither too fast to be perceived, nor so slow as to create drag) to optimize object constancy tracking and cognitive load reduction during interactive updates.
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Animation timing study (within-subjects, n=20+) testing MetroGraph's canvas transitions at 5 duration levels (200ms, 300ms, 400ms, 500ms, 800ms). Measure: (1) subjective smoothness rating (Likert), (2) task completion time (expect U-shaped curve, faster at 300-500ms), (3) comprehension accuracy (identify relationships in transformed graph), (4) perceived waiting time. Analyze eye-tracking data to confirm smooth pursuit eye movement at optimal duration.

design_hypotheses.statement: Text explanations alone (without interactive visualization) do not improve error detection or appropriately calibrate reliance; longer explanations may increase false confidence (mere exposure / completeness bias)
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: RCT: compare explanation-only vs. explanation + visualization + interaction; measure trust calibration (appropriately rejecting incorrect suggestions); task accuracy with incorrect agent advice; replication of Bansal finding (n>300, powered for interaction)

design_hypotheses.statement: Visualizing agent reasoning (showing decision steps, confidence, alternatives) reduces automation bias and increases appropriate reliance compared to opaque agent execution
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Controlled experiment measuring acceptance of incorrect agent suggestions; lower acceptance rate with transparency condition; eye-tracking showing increased attention to agent reasoning; error detection task performance improvement

design_hypotheses.statement: Making agent execution loops visible (step-by-step task execution, intermediate outputs, error handling) enables users to detect and correct agent failures faster than chat-based debugging or opaque agent logs
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Controlled experiment with error injection in agent workflows; measure time-to-detect-error, error correction success rate; compare graph-based workflow visualization vs. text logs vs. chat debugging; user study with domain experts (data engineers, workflow designers)

design_hypotheses.statement: Direct-manipulation graph interfaces (drag, click-to-expand, in-place edit) with visible agent actions produce lower cognitive load and better error detection than conversational chat + invisible agent execution
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: A/B test comparing graph canvas with visible agent nodes vs. chat-only interface; measure task completion time, error detection latency, mental model accuracy (simulation task); eye-tracking attention distribution

design_hypotheses.statement: Reducing edge crossings via orthogonal layout constraints will decrease cognitive load (measured by fixation duration, fixation count, pupil dilation) and improve comprehension accuracy compared to high-crossing layouts
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Eye-tracking study measuring fixation patterns and duration on metro-map vs force-directed layouts during path-finding and relationship identification tasks. Hypothesis validated if metro-map produces: (1) fewer fixations, (2) shorter average fixation duration, (3) higher comprehension accuracy (p<0.05).

design_hypotheses.statement: Reducing extraneous cognitive load through UI simplification (single-pane canvas, hide non-essential controls, minimize modal dialogs) will improve task performance more than increasing intrinsic load management
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Experiment comparing MetroGraph (high affordance, low extraneous load) vs. competitor tools (multiple panes, modal dialogs). Measure: task completion time, error rate, NASA-TLX cognitive load subscales (specifically extraneous load perception). Validated if MetroGraph significantly improves extraneous load scores and task performance.

design_hypotheses.statement: Metro-map style layouts (orthogonal edges, constrained routing, stable spatial encoding) will produce faster task completion and higher accuracy than force-directed layouts in database schema exploration tasks
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Controlled experiment comparing metro-map layout vs. force-directed layout on database schema comprehension tasks (identifying relationships, schema structure, cardinality constraints). Measure: task completion time, error rate, NASA-TLX cognitive load score. Hypothesis validated if metro-map shows significant (p<0.05) advantage on 2+ metrics.

design_hypotheses.statement: Progressive disclosure of graph nodes (showing related nodes on-demand, hiding non-essential relationships initially) will improve mental model formation and schema comprehension compared to full graph expansion
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Experiment comparing full-graph view vs. progressive-disclosure view. Measure: (1) Schema comprehension test (draw relationships, identify cardinality), (2) task completion time, (3) number of interactions needed, (4) confidence ratings. Validated if progressive-disclosure achieves higher comprehension scores without increased completion time.

design_hypotheses.statement: Stable spatial encoding in database schema visualizations (consistent node positions, fixed layout) will enable rapid recognition and enable knowledge transfer to future schema exploration tasks
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Longitudinal study: users explore same database schema multiple times. Measure: (1) task completion time improvement across sessions (learning curve), (2) accuracy improvement, (3) transfer test on new schema with similar structure. Validated if users show significant learning curve on repeated schemas and transfer to novel schemas faster than baseline.

design_hypotheses.statement: Strong visual affordances (directional arrows, color-coded interactive regions, expand/collapse affordances) will reduce training time and enable naive users to explore database schemas without prior instruction
design_hypotheses.what_would_validate: Between-subjects experiment: (1) high-affordance group (MetroGraph), (2) weak-affordance group (minimalist layout). Measure: time-to-first-interaction, task success rate on unprompted exploration, and success on targeted tasks without training. Validated if high-affordance group achieves significantly higher success rates and lower time-to-completion without training.

theory_grounding.claim: Direct-manipulation interfaces (drag, click, in-place edit) with visible affordances reduce cognitive load and enable faster mental model formation compared to conversational interfaces where agents execute invisibly

Users can only detect and correct agent errors when agent execution steps are observable; invisible agent execution (text logs, chat only) prevents timely error detection and enables persistence of undetected failures

Animation serves four primary functions in visualization: (1) object constancy tracking, (2) attentional cueing, (3) temporal relationship encoding, (4) exploratory interaction support. Effectiveness depends on timing (300-500ms optimal), continuity, and alignment with user mental models.

Cognitive Load Theory: Extraneous load (imposed by poor interface design) can be reduced through progressive disclosure, spatial integration, and redundancy elimination, freeing working memory for germane load (meaningful schema construction).

Split-Attention Effect: When essential information is spatially separated (diagram and text in different locations), cognitive load increases because users must maintain multiple sources in working memory and mentally integrate them. Physical integration (spatial proximity) or modality alignment (picture + spoken narrative) eliminates the effect.

Progressive Disclosure & Element Interactivity: High element interactivity (many interconnected elements requiring simultaneous processing) demands decomposition strategies like progressive disclosure or detail-on-demand to prevent cognitive overload.

Visualization Navigation: Focus+context and overview+detail interfaces outperform pure zooming for navigation tasks; users require both contextual awareness and detail focus, and simultaneous visibility of both reduces cognitive load compared to temporal switching.

Information Foraging Theory: Users navigate complex information spaces based on proximal information cues (information scent). Weak scent leads to high abandonment rates. Clear labels, familiar affordances, and predictable spatial layout provide strong information scent, enabling successful navigation without cognitive overload.

Redundancy Principle: Presenting the same information in multiple formats (text + diagram, picture + text redundantly) reduces learning and performance by consuming working memory resources. Elimination of redundancy is one of the highest-impact design principles.

Measurement of Cognitive Load: Subjective mental effort rating scales (Paas 9-point scale) are reliable, sensitive, and valid measures of cognitive load imposed by interface design. Physiological measures (eye-tracking, EEG) correlate with subjective load and validate scale accuracy.
Transparency of agent reasoning and decision steps reduces automation bias and complacency by enabling users to scrutinize agent recommendations rather than accepting them uncritically

Textual explanations increase user trust and recommendation acceptance but do not improve task accuracy or error detection; explanations can increase false confidence (mere exposure effect, completeness bias) leading to over-reliance

Mixed-initiative systems (human + AI agent) require visualization of agent state, reasoning, and action sequences to prevent inappropriate reliance and enable error detection; pure conversational chat obscures agent execution and leads to either over-reliance or distrust

User trust in AI systems is often miscalibrated (over-trust or under-trust) and depends on accuracy, transparency format, and domain expertise; one-size-fits-all explanations fail to calibrate trust effectively

Greater model interpretability does not automatically increase user reliance, comprehension, or decision accuracy; explanation complexity can increase cognitive load and reduce mental model quality; interpretability must be matched to user expertise level
Animated transitions maintain object constancy and help viewers track entity identity across transformations, reducing cognitive load required to update mental models of graph state.

Visual encodings processed preattentively (<250ms: color, size, position, orientation) enable rapid pattern recognition and anomaly detection without conscious effort, improving task efficiency by 5-10x over attentional encodings.

Users rely on information scent (proximal visual cues: labels, color, spatial proximity) to predict content relevance before navigation. Higher information scent reduces trial-and-error exploration; weak scent drives users to alternative interaction modes (chat, search).

Extraneous cognitive load (UI complexity, split attention, visual clutter) reduces working memory availability for germane load (meaningful learning). Spatially-separated information imposes 25-40% performance penalty.
Visual clutter in dense graphs (>30 nodes) exceeds working memory capacity, degrading comprehension accuracy and increasing task completion time
User reading patterns and visual attention sequences vary systematically based on graph layout structure, affecting comprehension speed and accuracy
Progressive disclosure (detail-on-demand, iterative expansion) prevents cognitive overload and improves schema comprehension compared to full graph expansion
Graph layout aesthetics (edge crossing, node overlap, aspect ratio) directly impact cognitive load and task completion time in comprehension tasks
Graph representation effectiveness (node-link vs matrix) is task-dependent; matrix superior for most tasks except path-finding
Minimizing edge crossings in graph layouts reduces visual clutter and improves comprehension task performance
